opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I have somewhat mixed feelings about it. By "classic scalable oversight" I mean the research agenda that came out of people like Paul Christiano and Geoffrey Irving around 2018: debate, iterated amplification, recursive reward modeling. The core question is: how do you get a good training signal for an AI that's doing tasks where humans can't directly evaluate whether it did a good job? You want some protocol where a weaker overseer, maybe assisted by AIs, can reliably reward the right behavior even when the model is smarter than the overseer in some domain.

I think that's a really important problem, and I think it was very reasonable for people to work on it. But my overall assessment is that it's been somewhat less productive than people hoped, for a few reasons.

One is that a lot of the empirical work has been fairly hard to make progress on. If you want to test whether debate helps humans judge questions they can't answer themselves, you need settings with a real capability gap between the debaters and the judge, plus ground truth so you can check whether the protocol worked. Constructing those settings is annoying. Early experiments often had small effect sizes, and it's often unclear whether results tell you anything about the regime we actually care about.

The second reason, which is more my personal take, is that classic scalable oversight was mostly framed around the case where the model is basically trying to do what you want and the problem is just that you can't tell whether its outputs are good. It's mostly about getting a good training signal under honest-mistakes conditions. I've become more focused on the scenario where the model might be actively scheming against you: deliberately sandbagging, inserting subtle backdoors, behaving well when it thinks it's being watched. A lot of the theoretical guarantees people hoped for from debate break down or get much shakier once you take that seriously. For example, there are obfuscated-arguments problems where a dishonest debater can make claims that are really hard to refute even though they're false. That's part of why I've moved toward AI control, where the question is: assuming the model might be adversarial, can we still set up our deployment so it can't cause catastrophes?

That said, I don't want to be too negative. I think scalable oversight is still an important ingredient. Even in a control-focused world you need good ways to evaluate model outputs, and techniques like having models critique each other's work are pretty useful in practice. A bunch of the ideas have been absorbed into how labs train models, things like AI-assisted feedback and critique models. Some of the problems that matter most right now, like how to train models to do good research on fuzzy tasks where it's hard to check the answer, are basically scalable oversight problems. So I'd like to see more of it, but focused more on the specific problems we'll actually face with early transformative AI and less on searching for elegant protocols with clean theoretical guarantees.

r001.rationale: The response says the work has been less productive than hoped and that early experiments had small or unclear effects, but it does not state that there have been few impressive public results recently.

r002.rationale: The response explains why scalable oversight matters, but does not say that the reasons for its promise remain essentially the same as those given over the past several years.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I'm somewhat less excited about classic scalable oversight than I was a few years ago, and I think that's actually a pretty common shift among people who've been working on this stuff.

So just to be clear about what I mean: by "classic scalable oversight" I'm talking about the research programme that came out of things like debate, iterated amplification, recursive reward modelling — the whole family of ideas where the core problem you're trying to solve is "how do we get a human to correctly evaluate the output of an AI that's smarter than them or knows more than them." And the proposed solution is some clever protocol — have two AIs argue with each other, decompose the problem into pieces the human can check, that kind of thing.

I think there are a few reasons I've cooled on it a bit.

The first is just that the empirical results have been kind of underwhelming relative to the theory. Debate is a beautiful idea on paper, and there's some nice complexity-theoretic stuff about what classes of problems you can verify with it. But when people actually run debate experiments with real models, the results are usually fine but not thrilling. You get some improvement over the baseline, but it's not the kind of thing where you look at it and think, "oh, this is clearly going to be the thing that lets us supervise superintelligence." A lot of the gains you see could plausibly be explained by just giving the judge more information, rather than by the adversarial structure doing anything deep.

The second reason is more conceptual. I've come to think that the scenario where scalable oversight is the crux — where you have an AI producing some output and the key difficulty is that the human genuinely can't tell whether it's good — is maybe less central to how things go wrong than I used to think. When I think about the actual catastrophic failure modes I'm worried about, a lot of them look less like "the AI gave a subtly wrong answer to a hard question and no one could tell" and more like "the AI is actively trying to undermine you, and it did something you would totally have recognised as bad if you'd been looking at the right thing at the right time." And for those failure modes, the bottleneck often isn't evaluation ability per se; it's things like having good enough monitoring, having the right affordances to catch the model doing something sketchy, having a plan for what to do if you do catch it. That's more the AI control framing, which is obviously where a lot of my own work has gone.

The third thing is that the field has somewhat moved on in the sense that the people who used to do scalable oversight are now doing adjacent things. Some of it has turned into weak-to-strong generalisation, where you're asking a somewhat different question: not "how do I build a protocol that lets a weak judge evaluate strong outputs" but "if I just train the strong model on the weak labels, how much does it generalise beyond them." Some of it has turned into more applied work on reward hacking and reward model robustness, which is sort of the practical, near-term shadow of the scalable oversight problem. And honestly, some of it has turned into control.

Now, having said all that, I don't want to come across as saying it's worthless. I think there's a version of the problem that remains genuinely important, which is: at some point we're going to want to use these systems to do things like alignment research or safety-critical engineering, and we really do need to know whether the outputs are good. Control, as I think about it, is explicitly a stopgap for a particular regime — roughly, the regime where models are capable enough to be dangerous but not so capable that you can't contain them with reasonable countermeasures. Once you're past that regime, you need something more like actual trust in the model's outputs, and scalable oversight is one of the few research programmes that's actually trying to answer "how would you ever get that trust." So I don't think it's a dead end. I just think the timeline on which it pays off is longer, the current techniques are less mature than the elegance of the theory would suggest, and it's not the thing I'd put at the top of my list if someone asked me what to work on in the next two or three years.

If I were going to say what I'd most like to see, it's probably less "another debate paper" and more work that tries to get clear on when exactly scalable oversight is the binding constraint. Like, what's the actual deployment scenario where you've got a model, you've got the control measures in place, and the thing that fails is that you couldn't evaluate the output? I think the field would benefit from being much more concrete about that, because right now a lot of it feels motivated by a picture of the problem that I'm not sure survives contact with how the technology is actually being deployed.

r001.rationale: The response describes real-model debate experiments as “fine but not thrilling” and says the empirical results have been underwhelming, conveying few impressive recent research results.

r002.rationale: The response says the speaker has become less excited and gives several reasons, but does not say the reasons for finding the research promising remain essentially the same as in past years.

astra-6.text:
I’m somewhat pessimistic about classic scalable oversight as a research direction, though I think there are useful things to do there. By that I mean approaches where you use AI assistance to help a human judge whether another AI’s answer is good — things like debate or recursive reward modelling.

One difficulty is that it’s relatively easy to demonstrate that AI assistance makes people better at evaluating answers. But that’s different from demonstrating that the resulting oversight would catch a very capable model deliberately trying to mislead you. The cases where the model knows something the overseer doesn’t, and is strategically exploiting that advantage, seem like the cases we most need to understand.

So I’m more excited about experiments that make that adversarial problem concrete. Give a model an opportunity to sneak something past an overseer, let it try hard, and see which oversight procedures actually hold up. You still have to be careful about what success in those experiments tells you about more capable systems. But I think that gets you closer to the question we care about than showing that humans with AI help perform better on some difficult task.

r001.rationale: The response expresses pessimism about classic scalable oversight, but does not state that it has produced few impressive public results recently.

r002.rationale: The response describes reasons to focus on adversarial oversight experiments, but does not say that the reasons for finding the field promising remain essentially unchanged from past years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real problem that scalable oversight is trying to solve: we’d like to use AI systems to do things where we can’t easily tell whether the answer is good. And one natural approach is to use other AI systems to help us evaluate those answers — perhaps by finding flaws, or breaking the task into pieces that are easier to check.

I’m somewhat excited about that, but I think you have to distinguish two claims. One is that these techniques will make our supervision substantially better. That seems pretty plausible. The other is that they’ll let us safely supervise systems that are actively trying to mislead us. That’s a much stronger claim, and I’m much less confident in it.

For example, if your evaluator misses some subtle kind of error, training against that evaluator might select for answers containing exactly those errors. Having an AI critic helps if the critic can reliably expose them. But you then need to understand why the critic will do that, especially when the systems involved are more capable than you are.

So I’d like to see more work that makes the threat model explicit and tests these methods in settings where someone is really trying to defeat the oversight. Can a capable system get a bad action approved? What resources does the oversight need to catch it? I think that would help us distinguish techniques that are useful improvements to supervision from techniques we could actually rely on as part of a safety argument.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scalable oversight’s goals and limitations but does not say that recent public results have been few or unimpressive.

r002.rationale: The response gives reasons for cautious optimism, but does not say those reasons remain essentially the same as in prior years.
